fields.meta_title: Employee Information Form That Stays Current | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What goes on an employee information form, what payroll needs from it, and an app that asks every employee to confirm their record each year.
fields.h1: Build an Employee Information Form That Stays Current
fields.hero_description: Build an employee information form that keeps one record per person and asks each employee to confirm it every year.
fields.features_heading: A Staff Record That Does Not Go Stale
fields.features_subheading: A signed sheet in a folder is right on the day it was filled in. Emergent's version asks again every year and routes each change.
fields.feature_1:
One record per employee

Saves every answer to one row per person in a database you own, with the date each field last changed. Payroll and benefits forms later pull their details from that same row.
fields.feature_2:
Yearly confirmation, pre-filled

Sends each employee their current record once a year with every answer already in place. They confirm it or edit a line, and anyone who has not replied gets an email reminder.
fields.feature_3:
Changes routed to payroll

Posts each edit to a legal name or tax state to payroll as a direct message showing the old value next to the new one. Payroll applies it from the date the change takes effect.
fields.feature_4:
Missing fields found and requested

Scans imported records for blank required fields and sends each affected person a short link for only what is missing. HR watches the open count drop as answers come in.
fields.feature_5:
Each role sees its own fields

Shows a store manager the work phones of their own team and nothing more personal. Pay details and Social Security numbers open only for the HR and payroll roles you name.
fields.feature_6:
The app's code, in your repo

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub on paid plans. An engineer can sync employee records with your payroll provider or HRIS over its API, or you describe the sync to Emergent.

fields.tab_content_1:
Every record sent, 112 back in ten days

January is when the records get checked. Northwind Freight sends each of its 140 employees their own record, every field filled in from last year. Most people confirm without changing a thing, and a driver who moved in the spring fixes his address. After ten days 112 have replied, and the other 28 get an email reminder.
fields.tab_content_2:
The new surname waits on a Social Security card

Marriage changes a surname, and payroll has to time the switch. Lena Park, a supervisor at Northwind Freight, submits her new last name, Ortiz. Her Social Security card does not show it yet, and payroll keeps Park on file until it does. Once she shows HR the new card, payroll gets a direct message to change the name.
fields.tab_content_3:
Seventeen links, each one asking for less

Old spreadsheets hide gaps. Bayside Dental moves 86 staff records into the app, and 17 come in without a home address or a personal phone. Instead of a full form, each of those people gets a link that asks only for their missing fields. By Friday 11 have filled the gap, and HR sees 6 still open.
fields.tab_content_4:
Managers see phones, and HR sees the rest

Store managers need a phone number, not a birth date. At Juniper Home Goods, each one opens a directory of their own team with a work phone beside every name. Home addresses and birth dates stay in the HR view. A manager who needs an address for a mailing asks HR, and the request is logged.

fields.howto_title: How to Make an Employee Information Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan an employee information form that gives payroll what it needs and stays current year after year.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Fill in what you already know
fields.howto_step_1_des: Payroll is the strictest reader of the form. Ask for the legal name as printed on the Social Security card, with a separate field for the name the person goes by. Every other field serves HR or a manager. Add one only when someone will use it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Group the questions under personal details, contact details, job details and emergency contacts. One section per screen keeps the form short on a phone, and HR can later resend a single section when only that part needs an update.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Flag the Social Security number, birth date and home address as HR-only before anyone fills the form in. Decide now which roles see which fields, because pulling a detail back after it has been shared widely is hard.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pre-fill the job title, reporting line and start date from your own HR records, then let each employee check them. People spot a wrong title in seconds, and nobody has to retype facts HR already holds.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Split employee edits from HR edits
fields.howto_step_5_des: Let employees change their own contact details and emergency contacts directly. A new job title or pay rate goes through HR instead, because it comes from a decision someone else made, not from the employee.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose a quiet month, away from open enrollment and year-end payroll. Give people a deadline of about two weeks and send one reminder before it. Anyone still unconfirmed after the deadline goes on a short follow-up list for HR.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Send a new home address to payroll and a new phone number to the manager. Keep each old value with the date it changed. A returned letter or a W-2 mailed to the wrong address can then be traced.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is printable PDFs, payroll checklists and template pages that collect an employee's details once, at hiring, then file them. The record goes stale: an address from two moves ago, a surname payroll changed too early, a phone nobody answers. This page covers what the form holds and what payroll needs, then builds what a PDF cannot: a record every employee confirms each year, edits that route to payroll on the right terms, gaps found and filled, and views that show each role only its fields. Onboarding paperwork stays with the new employee form page.
tab_stories: Every January a freight company sends each of its 140 employees their own record pre-filled, and by day 10 there are 112 confirmations, while the other 28 get a reminder.
A warehouse supervisor marries and submits a new surname, and payroll keeps the old name on file until she shows HR her updated Social Security card, then gets a direct message to change it.
A dental group moves 86 records out of an old spreadsheet, 17 turn out to lack a home address or a personal phone, and each of those 17 people gets a link that asks only for the missing fields.
A store manager opens the team directory and sees a work phone beside every name, while home addresses and birth dates stay in the HR view.

chip_prompts: Pre-fill each employee's record with the job title and start date I already have on file. They should only need to check those and add their own contact details.
Every January, email each employee the record HR holds for them and ask them to confirm it or correct any field. Remind anyone who has not answered after ten days.
When someone edits their legal name or tax state, message my payroll lead directly with the before and after values and the date the change applies from.
Give each store manager a list of their own team's names and work phones. Social Security numbers and home addresses should stay in a view that only HR and payroll can open.

specificity.evidence: HR and payroll vocabulary: 'legal name as printed on the Social Security card', 'Form W-4', 'Form I-9', 'tax state', 'W-2 mailed to the wrong address'.

craft.evidence: QC Q-checks clean; no blocking craft class.

truth.evidence: Name-change rule matches IRS Pub 15 (old name until the updated card is shown); W-4 and SSN-from-card match IRS hiring page; I-9 matches USCIS; numbers agree (97+15+28=140, 11+6=17, 86-17=69).

distinct.evidence: Record-maintenance angle (annual check, name change, gaps, role views) differs from new-employee-form's onboarding packet tabs.
